title: Title
notes: Open Appendix 02 as a change in medium. The printed appendix offers finite lookup tables; the notebook turns those lookup ideas into reproducible functions, simulations, and diagnostics that can be queried at the sample size and error level actually needed.

title: Route
notes: Use this route to orient the lecture around operations rather than page references. Each historical table can be translated into a mathematical query, then the notebook supplies a computation, a visual sanity check, and a small audit record.

title: Table Entry As Query
notes: Pause on the phrase table entry as query. A lookup table hides its construction, while an executable replacement makes the random variable, tail probability, model assumption, and numerical tolerance visible to the learner. That visibility is what allows students to critique the answer instead of merely locating it.

title: Von Mises Quantiles
notes: This slide connects the first replacement to model geometry. The number that used to live in a chart is the angular half-width needed to hold a selected probability under a von Mises density with a given concentration.

title: Bessel Ratio Inverse
notes: Here the table replacement is an inverse function. Students should see that concentration estimation is stable only because the Bessel ratio is monotone, and that the notebook checks this property numerically instead of trusting a black-box interpolation.

title: Reporting Kappa
notes: The reporting slide translates an inverse calculation into language a statistician can use. The estimate is not just a number; it tells how tightly a unimodal circular model would concentrate probability near the fitted direction.

title: Simulated Uniformity Values
notes: This is the cleanest example of replacing a table by a reproducible reference experiment. The simulation creates the null distribution at the requested sample size, and the critical value is just the appropriate tail quantile.

title: Four Statistics
notes: The table of test types helps prevent a one-test-fits-all interpretation. The appendix contains several critical-value replacements because circular non-uniformity can appear as a mean direction, a CDF discrepancy, an unusual gap pattern, or a compressed range.

title: Critical Surface
notes: The surface slide makes the advantage of computation visible. Instead of reading a single cell, students inspect the shape of the reference family and can ask how much the critical value changes with sample size or alpha.

title: Kappa Confidence Bands
notes: The concentration chart is useful because it turns estimator variability into a visible band. The lesson is not a particular printed value; it is how the uncertainty in kappa estimation contracts with more observations. Ask students to compare the two bands before naming any formula.

title: Executable Panel
notes: This slide names the interface contract for a good table replacement. The user should never receive a naked number; they should receive the inputs, the computed answer, the visual context, and enough provenance to rerun or audit the calculation.

title: Guardrails
notes: The guardrails are the reason an executable appendix can be more trustworthy than a copied table. If an interpolation, simulation, or inversion routine breaks a basic ordering property, the notebook should fail loudly before a learner uses the result.

title: Worked Mini Lab
notes: The mini lab is deliberately framed as a recipe students can rerun. It separates the statistic, the null simulation, the quantile extraction, and the decision comparison, so the old table is replaced by a transparent computational experiment.

title: Notebook Artifacts
notes: Connect the lecture back to the notebook artifacts without turning the slide into a file listing. The important point is that each artifact teaches a replacement strategy and each check records a property that the replacement must preserve.

title: Recap
notes: Close by asking learners to design the interface for a table replacement before computing anything. If they can name the statistic, inputs, tail, output, visual diagnostic, and check, they understand the appendix as a reproducible method rather than a catalog of numbers.
